name: Prolog
year_note: Philippe Roussel implemented the first Prolog system (in Algol-W) in the fall of 1972, although the abstract of Colmerauer and Roussel's own history dates the preliminary version to late 1971. The simplified, definitive Fortran interpreter followed in 1973; the 'Edinburgh' syntax used today comes from DEC-10 Prolog (1975–77).
organization: University of Aix-Marseille (Artificial Intelligence Group, Luminy)
tagline: Programming in logic: state facts and rules, then ask questions and let unification and backtracking find the answers.
summary: Prolog is a logic programming language in which a program is a set of facts and rules (Horn clauses) and running it means posing a query that the system proves by resolution. Unification matches and builds terms, and depth-first search with backtracking enumerates every solution, so the same relation can often be run 'forwards' or 'backwards'. It became the standard language of logic programming and a mainstay of symbolic AI, natural-language processing and expert systems.
history:
Prolog grew out of Alain Colmerauer's natural-language question-answering work at Marseille, where he had earlier built the Q-systems rewriting language for machine translation. After Robert Kowalski visited Marseille in 1971, the group adopted a restricted form of his SL-resolution theorem-proving procedure, unifying only with clause heads. In the fall of 1972 Philippe Roussel implemented the first Prolog system in Algol-W, and a 610-clause French man–machine dialogue system became the first large Prolog program; a simplified, definitive interpreter was written in Fortran in 1973 by Gérard Battani, Henry Meloni and René Bazzoli. Kowalski supplied the theory: the procedural interpretation of Horn clauses (1974).

David H. D. Warren took Prolog to Edinburgh, where DEC-10 Prolog (1975–77) added the first Prolog compiler and the 'Edinburgh syntax' that later systems follow; his 1983 Warren Abstract Machine became the standard blueprint for implementations. Japan's Fifth Generation Computer Systems project (1982) chose logic programming as its basis, and Prolog was standardized as ISO/IEC 13211-1 in 1995, with modules (2000) and definite clause grammars (2025) as later parts. Modern systems such as SWI-Prolog, SICStus, GNU Prolog and Scryer add constraint solving, tabling, modules and threads.
innovations: Logic programming: a program is a set of Horn clauses and running it is proving a query
Unification as the single mechanism for parameter passing, pattern matching and building data
Built-in depth-first search with backtracking, with the cut (!) to prune the search
Relations that can be queried in several directions, with no fixed inputs and outputs
Definite clause grammars: grammar rules that translate directly into parsers
The Warren Abstract Machine (1983), the template for efficient logic-language compilers

typing.notes: Every value is a term (atom, number, variable or compound); Wikipedia describes Prolog as untyped. ISO built-ins check argument types at run time and raise type_error.

influenced_by_external.name: Q-systems
influenced_by_external.note: Colmerauer's tree-rewriting language for machine translation; Prolog began as an attempt to write a whole question-answering system in logic instead.

influenced_by_external.name: SL-resolution (Kowalski & Kuehner)
influenced_by_external.note: The resolution strategy that, restricted to Horn clauses (SLD-resolution), became Prolog's execution model.

influenced_by_external.name: Resolution principle (J. A. Robinson)
influenced_by_external.note: Resolution with unification, the basis of automated theorem proving.

influenced_by_external.name: Planner
influenced_by_external.note: Hewitt's goal-directed AI language; Kowalski's work reconciled its procedural approach with logic.

influenced_by_external.name: Floyd's nondeterministic algorithms
influenced_by_external.note: Backtracking 'à la Floyd' was adopted to implement the search efficiently.

logic-unification.note: Programs are Horn clauses executed by SLD-resolution: unification plus depth-first backtracking.

recursion.note: The only looping construct besides backtracking.

pattern-matching.note: Clause heads are matched by two-way unification, which subsumes one-way pattern matching.

tail-calls.note: Last-call optimization in WAM-based systems (DEC-10 Prolog had it by 1980), so recursive loops run in constant stack.

structured-control.note: Conjunction, disjunction, if-then-else (C -> T ; E) and negation as failure; iteration is recursion or failure-driven backtracking.

generators.note: Any nondeterministic predicate (e.g. between/3, member/2) yields its solutions one at a time on backtracking.

coroutines.note: Coroutining via delayed goals (freeze/2, dif/2) in most systems; not part of ISO.

immutability.note: Terms are immutable and logic variables are bound once (undone on backtracking); assert/retract mutate only the clause database.

list-comprehensions.note: findall/3, bagof/3 and setof/3 collect all solutions of a goal, set-builder style.

declarative-queries.note: Facts form a relational database queried by goals, but the search order is fixed by the program (the root of Datalog).

first-class-functions.note: Goals are terms that can be passed and invoked with call/N (maplist/3 etc.); no closures in ISO, though SWI-Prolog's library(yall) adds lambdas.

homoiconicity.note: Clauses are ordinary terms: a :- b is the term ':-'(a, b).

reflection.note: clause/2, assert/retract, functor/3 and =../2 inspect and rewrite the running program.

macros.note: term_expansion/2 and goal_expansion/2 rewrite clauses at load time (de facto standard, not ISO).

modules.note: Not in early Prologs or the ISO core; the ISO module standard (13211-2, 2000) is little used, and systems ship their own (Quintus/SWI-style) module systems.

hot-code-reload.note: Reconsulting a file (SWI-Prolog's make/0) redefines predicates in the running system.

garbage-collection.note: DEC-10 Prolog gained a garbage collector by 1980.

milestones.event: Robert Kowalski visits Marseille; SL-resolution is adopted for Colmerauer's question-answering project
Roussel implements the first Prolog system in Algol-W; the language is named
Definitive Marseille Prolog interpreter written in Fortran (Battani, Meloni, Bazzoli)
Kowalski's 'Predicate Logic as Programming Language' gives the procedural interpretation of Horn clauses
Warren, Pereira and Pereira describe DEC-10 Prolog, the first Prolog compiler, in Edinburgh
Japan's Fifth Generation Computer Systems project adopts logic programming
David H. D. Warren describes the Warren Abstract Machine (WAM)
ISO/IEC TS 13211-3 standardizes definite clause grammar rules

trivia: The name, an abbreviation of 'PROgrammation en LOGique', was suggested by Philippe Roussel's wife.
Warren carried Prolog from Marseille to Edinburgh as a large deck of punched cards.
The 1973 Marseille interpreter dropped the unification 'occur check' as too costly; standard Prolog still omits it, offering unify_with_occurs_check/2 separately.

hello.code:
% A program is a set of clauses; running it means posing a query: ?- main.
main :-
    write('Hello, World!'), nl.
hello.notes: The runner consults the file and poses the query ?- main. (swipl -g main -t halt). The ':-' clause notation is the Edinburgh (DEC-10) syntax adopted by ISO; the original Marseille Prolog marked literals with + and - signs instead.

factorial.code:
% factorial(N, F) is a relation between N and F, not a function.
factorial(0, 1).
factorial(N, F) :-
    N > 0,
    N1 is N - 1,
    factorial(N1, F1),
    F is N * F1.

main :-
    factorial(10, F),
    write(F), nl.
factorial.notes: Arithmetic is not evaluated by unification: is/2 must be called explicitly. SWI-Prolog integers are unbounded.

fizzbuzz.code:
% The first clause whose guard succeeds wins; the cut (!) commits to it.
fizzbuzz(N, 'FizzBuzz') :- N mod 15 =:= 0, !.
fizzbuzz(N, 'Fizz')     :- N mod 3 =:= 0, !.
fizzbuzz(N, 'Buzz')     :- N mod 5 =:= 0, !.
fizzbuzz(N, N).

% A failure-driven loop: fail forces backtracking into between/3.
main :-
    (   between(1, 15, N),
        fizzbuzz(N, Out),
        write(Out), nl,
        fail
    ;   true
    ).
fizzbuzz.expected_output:
1
2
Fizz
4
Buzz
Fizz
7
8
Fizz
Buzz
11
Fizz
13
14
FizzBuzz
fizzbuzz.notes: The failure-driven loop (Goal, fail ; true) is classic Prolog iteration. between/3 is not in the ISO core but every major system provides it.

higher-order.code:
% findall/3 is Prolog's comprehension: collect every Y the goal can prove.
main :-
    findall(Y, ( between(1, 10, X), X mod 2 =:= 0, Y is X * X ), Ys),
    print_spaced(Ys).

print_spaced([X]) :- write(X), nl.
print_spaced([X, Y | Rest]) :-
    write(X), write(' '),
    print_spaced([Y | Rest]).
higher-order.notes: findall/3 (ISO) collects every solution of a goal. SWI-Prolog also has include/3, maplist/3 and yall lambdas: maplist([X,Y]>>(Y is X*X), Evens, Squares).

shapes.code:
% Shapes are plain terms; clauses dispatch by unifying on their structure.
area(rectangle(W, H), A) :- A is W * H.
area(triangle(B, H), A)  :- A is B * H // 2.

label(rectangle(_, _), 'Rectangle').
label(triangle(_, _), 'Triangle').

main :-
    forall(member(S, [rectangle(3, 4), triangle(10, 3)]),
           ( label(S, Name), area(S, A),
             write(Name), write(': '), write(A), nl )).
shapes.notes: No classes or declared types: shapes are compound terms and area/2 picks its clause by unifying the head. forall/2 and member/2 are de facto standard library predicates.

signature.title: Facts, rules and backtracking
signature.code:
% Facts: a small family tree.
parent(tom, bob).
parent(tom, liz).
parent(bob, ann).
parent(bob, pat).
parent(pat, jim).

% Rules: ancestor is the transitive closure of parent.
ancestor(X, Y) :- parent(X, Y).
ancestor(X, Y) :- parent(X, Z), ancestor(Z, Y).

% Queries: backtracking enumerates every solution, in either direction.
main :-
    write('Descendants of tom:'),
    ( ancestor(tom, D), write(' '), write(D), fail ; nl ),
    write('Ancestors of jim:'),
    ( ancestor(A, jim), write(' '), write(A), fail ; nl ).
signature.expected_output:
Descendants of tom: bob liz ann pat jim
Ancestors of jim: pat tom bob
signature.notes: One ancestor/2 relation answers both 'who descends from tom?' and 'who are jim's ancestors?'. The answer order follows Prolog's depth-first, left-to-right search. The family tree is adapted from Ivan Bratko's textbook 'Prolog Programming for Artificial Intelligence'.
